item.text: [{"taxonId":48624,"summary":"A genus of flowering plants native to Europe, Asia and Africa, with some species naturalized in North America. Most are aromatic herbaceous perennials, though some are annuals, and their tubular flowers range from lavender and blue to white, pink or lilac. Some species contain nepetalactone, which can cause temporary euphoria in cats.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p3","s1:p4","s1:p5","s1:p6"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":48628,"summary":"A genus of herbaceous flowering plants native only to eastern and central North America, especially prairies and open woodland. These drought-tolerant perennials bear large summer flower heads with a prominent spiny cone and outer florets that often droop, usually in pink or purple.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p5","s1:p7"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":48678,"summary":"A genus of mostly herbaceous perennial flowering plants native chiefly to North America, including Mexico, with a few species native to South America and Eurasia. Goldenrods usually bear many bright golden-yellow flower heads in late summer and can spread by wind-borne seed or underground rhizomes that form colonies.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"Young leaves are edible; herbal teas are sometimes made, and Native Americans traditionally ate seeds of some species.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p6"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p18"]}},{"taxonId":48681,"summary":"A genus of deciduous shrubs native to the temperate Northern Hemisphere, with greatest diversity in eastern Asia. They have simple, alternately arranged leaves and clusters of many small white, pink or reddish flowers; many species are grown ornamentally for these showy displays.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p5","s1:p6","s1:p12"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":48690,"summary":"A genus of perennial flowering plants native to North America, including Canada, the United States, Mexico and the Bahamas. They survive winter in underground corms and resprout, and some species are grown as ornamentals or cut for bouquets.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":48798,"summary":"A genus of annual or perennial flowering plants native to western and central North America. In mid- to late summer, clumps of toothed basal leaves send up upright stems topped with pink, white or purple five-petalled, mallow-like flowers.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p2"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":48801,"summary":"A genus of small deciduous trees or large shrubs native to warm-temperate parts of North America, southern Europe, western and central Asia, and China. Redbuds are memorable for rounded to heart-shaped leaves and pinkish-red flowers that appear in early spring on bare branches and even the trunk.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":48807,"summary":"An evergreen hardwood tree or shrub native to coastal forests and Sierra foothills of California, extending into southwestern Oregon and northwestern Baja California. Its bruised leaves smell strongly of camphor, and its purple-ripening fruit resembles a miniature avocado. Native Americans ate briefly ripe flesh and traditionally roasted the inner pit before eating it.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"Ripe flesh was eaten fresh or dried; pits were traditionally roasted before eating. Leaves have culinary use but contain high levels of toxic umbellulone.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p5","s1:p6","s1:p8","s1:p19","s1:p20"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p19","s1:p20","s1:p22"]}},{"taxonId":48865,"summary":"A large palm native to Southeast Asia, New Guinea and the southwestern Pacific, now widespread along tropical coasts. Its fibrous fruit contains coconut water and edible flesh, while the flesh also yields coconut milk and oil; the husk supplies coir and the hard shell can become charcoal.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"Coconut water is drunk; immature flesh is eaten fresh, mature flesh is processed, and flesh yields milk and cooking oil. Sap is also consumed or fermented.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p3","s1:p8"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p3","s1:p100","s1:p101","s1:p102","s1:p103"]}},{"taxonId":48890,"summary":"A one-species genus of trees native to tropical dry forests of Africa. Its African tulip tree bears conspicuous reddish-orange or crimson cup-shaped flowers that hold rain and dew, while the water-filled buds can squirt when handled. Widely planted across the tropics, it has become invasive in several regions.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p3","s1:p5","s1:p9"],"humanEdibility":[]}}]
